title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
What is pollination?
≈ 1 min




Pollen is producedin the anthers



›




An animal carries itto another flower



›




It must land on a stigmaof the same species




→ fertilisation → seeds


For the non-specialists: plants cannot move, so to mate they need a courier. Pollen from one flower has to reach the stigma of another flower of the same species. Pollen landing on the wrong species is lost, and can even block the stigma. The three photos are from our meadow: Succisa anther, a hoverfly (Eristalis interruptus) covered in pollen, a Succisa stigma.

Why does it matter?
≈ 1.5 min



≈ 88 %


of flowering plants are pollinated by animals


Ollerton, Winfree, and Tarrant (2011)




75 %


of leading crop types benefit from animal pollination


Klein et al. (2007)




5–8 %


of global crop production, US$ 235–577 billion per year


Potts et al. (2016)





Pollinators are declining, and most pollination happensin diverse communities where plants share their pollinators.



Ollerton et al. 2011: about 87.5 % of flowering plant species are animal-pollinated (higher in the tropics, about 78 % in temperate communities). Klein et al. 2007: 87 of 115 leading global food crops (75 %) benefit from animal pollination. Potts et al. 2016 (IPBES assessment): 5–8 % of global crop production is directly attributable to animal pollination, worth US$ 235–577 billion per year. Decline: e.g. Hallmann et al. 2017 found a more than 75 % drop in flying insect biomass over 27 years in German protected areas. Bridge: pollination is not one plant and one bee. In a meadow like ours, dozens of plants share the same insects. That is the starting point of our work.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Sharing is the norm
≈ 1.5 min


















Not only bees: in our meadow hoverflies, flies, beetles, butterflies and moths all visit flowers (photos: burnet moth on Sanguisorba, Eristalis on Achillea, butterflies on Succisa). In species-rich meadows most plants are generalists and share most of their visitors. Sharing is a problem for a plant: pollen is lost to other species (consumption, wrong stigmas) and foreign pollen arrives on its own stigma (heterospecific pollen, HP). Central question of the whole talk: how do plants in such a meadow still get enough of their own pollen (conspecific pollen, CP)?

The locality
≈ 1 min




Czech Republic

Study design: Janovský et al. (2013)


K Handrkovu near Vernýřov, Central Bohemia (49.8466 N, 15.1498 E). Moist to mesophilous grassland mosaic, two flowering peaks (May, August), mown twice a year. Sampling at the August peak. Where it started: Janovský et al. 2013 (PLoS ONE) set up the plot design and showed that conspecific and heterospecific flower densities at a scale of a few metres drive which pollinators visit a plant. This small-scale density effect comes back twice in this talk: dilution of foreign pollen on Succisa stigmas (Part 3) and the pull of the core species (Part 4).

text:
Why should timing matter?
≈ 1 min




< 1 %


of pollen reachesa conspecific stigma





Dose, don’t dump


small packages,many couriers


Pollen presentation theory





When = Who


timing selectsthe courier




Plants can’t choose visitors, but they can choose when


Transition to Part 2: we move from meadow-wide networks down to the scale of the pollen grain. 1. The dilemma: anthers produce millions of grains, but < 1% ever reaches a conspecific stigma. Over 99% is eaten by hoverflies and bees, groomed away, or dropped on foreign stigmas. 2. Harder & Thomson 1989: because visits have diminishing returns, dumping all pollen at once causes massive wastage. Dosing pollen gradually across visits maximizes the number of carriers and recipient mates. 3. In a shared meadow, pollinators have distinct daily activity curves. When a plant releases its pollen determines which pollinator guild it attracts and how much foreign pollen it avoids.

START I methods (Štenc et al. 2023, AJB): 15 and 16 August 2021, hourly sampling, 5 vials per species per hour, each vial = flowers from 5 random inflorescences (3 flowers for Trifolium and Centaurea, 5 for Succisa) in 2 ml of detergent with basic fuchsin. title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Who carries the pollen?
≈ 1 min

Individual body pollen loads across all flower visitors (618 individuals, 2 seasons)


 Martin FreudenfeldPhD student, Charles University



















618 pollinators, 2020–2021, Handrkov · Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Transition: In START II we examined 3 focal plant species. To test whether these dynamics hold across the whole community, Martin Freudenfeld conducted a comprehensive, meadow-wide scan of pollen loads across all flower visitors (618 pollinators across 35 insect groups). Pollen swabbed with fuchsin jelly from one half of the body; counts are per quarter of the body. Step 1: every dot is one insect. Loads range from a few grains to thousands within the same group. Step 2 (click): group means with 95 % CI. Groups do differ (ANOVA F(30, 531) = 21.3, p < 0.001, 54.6 % of variance), bees and large Eristalis carry most, Pieris and Coenonympha least. But most groups overlap broadly: the spread among individuals is as large as the spread among groups. Step 3 (click): coefficients of variation. CV among group means 0.75, median CV among individuals within a group 0.77. Knowing the group tells you little more than knowing the individual. Figure redrawn from raw data (35 groups); the paper’s model used 31 groups.

≈ 1 min













45 472 visits, 2011–2021 · Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Step 1: interaction density of dominant pollinator groups across years (2011–2021). Sarcophagidae, Apis and Sphaerophoria jump several-fold between consecutive years. Eristalis tenax is the most constant of the dominant groups. Step 2 (click): CV across years. title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Abundance, not identity
≈ 0.5 min






Coefficient of variation = SD / mean, i.e. spread relative to the average


Data: Freudenfeld et al. (2025)



Pollinators differ little in how much pollen they carry.Their contribution is set by how abundant they are that year.



Coefficients of variation: among group means of pollen load (0.75), median within-group CV of pollen load among individuals (0.77), median CV of visitation density among years within a group (1.13). Values computed for this slide from the paper’s data (scripts/fig_freudenfeld_2025.R). Conclusion of Freudenfeld et al. 2025: a pollinator’s contribution to pollen transfer depends more on its abundance than on its capacity to carry pollen. A diverse pollinator community buffers the decline of any single taxon. Bridge to Part 3: if many different, variable carriers deliver pollen, what finally arrives on the stigma?

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Many carriers, steadier delivery
≈ 1 min













Pollen transported = yearly visit density × mean pollen load of the group · 32 groups, 2011–2021 · data Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Combining the two datasets: yearly interaction density of each group (2011–2021) × its mean load per ¼ body (2020–2021). Assumes a group’s mean load is the same every year. Step 1: pollen transported per survey, stacked by group. The main carriers swap: Tenthredinidae in 2012, Sarcophagidae and Apis in 2019–2020. Step 2 (click): CV across years. Single groups 0.74–1.56 (median of all 32 groups 1.13, abundance-weighted mean 1.01); whole community 0.53. Synchrony among groups φ = 0.28 (Loreau & de Mazancourt; 1 = all groups move together), so groups largely compensate for each other. Caveat: the total visit density has almost the same CV (0.54), so the buffering comes from abundances, not from loads. Fits the stability theme of the deck: diverse carriers stabilise pollination. Script: scripts/fig_freud_more.R

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Preference and constancy
≈ 20 s








Field interview stick: offering two flowers to observe sequential foraging choices




Preference Which flower type is chosen more often than expected by chance (innate or learned bias).


Flower Constancy Fidelity across consecutive choices: sticking to the same species sequentially.


→ Constancy directly governs the purity of pollen carried on the body!




Quick mention / transition (≈ 20 s): “We also tested foraging decisions in the field using interview sticks. Briefly, preference is which flower an insect chooses, whereas constancy is whether it faithfully sticks to the same species across consecutive visits—which directly determines whether its pollen load remains pure. To test what governs these choices under strictly controlled conditions, we moved into the lab with 3D-printed flowers.”

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
How do pollinators choose?
≈ 1 min


3D-printed flowers, 3 % sucrose, Eristalis tenax · Matoušková, Štenc, and Janovský (2023); Haveldová et al. (submitted)


Bridge: the field tells us who visits. To see how an individual pollinator decides, we went to the lab. A: arena with two flower forms in a chessboard pattern, 15 cm apart, so the fly must fly between flowers. B: each flight is scored as constant (same form) or switching. C: four forms, yellow or white, large or small. D: in the field E. tenax visits mostly Succisa. E: in the fly’s colour space, the white form sits next to Succisa, Centaurea and Selinum, the yellow form next to Leontodon. So the artificial flowers mimic real core plants of the meadow. Matoušková et al. 2023 (Biol. J. Linn. Soc.): naive E. tenax select colour most strongly, then size, symmetry only weakly; yellow is preferred, especially when large.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Experience changes the choice
≈ 1 min










Naive flies (lab-reared): strong innate preference for yellow




Experienced flies (caught in the meadow): no colour preference left
Flower constancy 10–15 % lower after experience




5 270 visits by naive and 31 973 by experienced flies · Haveldová, Štenc, Matoušková & Janovský (submitted)


Share of all visits that went to yellow forms, summed over the four forms (naive: YL 1 829 + YS 1 682 of 4 841 visits; experienced: 8 000 + 7 855 of 31 973). Caveat: visits were not spread evenly across treatments, so this is a summary of the raw counts, not the model. The GLMs show significant colour, size and interaction effects in both groups (Table 1 of the manuscript). Experienced flies from a flower-rich meadow are more opportunistic: weaker preferences and lower constancy. They also reacted more to which flowers they could see from their position (angular area ratio). Implication for the plant: an experienced hoverfly arriving on Succisa has likely just visited something else.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Who stays faithful?
≈ 1 min







Hoverflies, the main visitors of Succisa,are among the least constant pollinators.



Field experiments at Handrkov, 25 pollinator species × plant-pair tests · Sedláčková (2024)


Share of foraging decisions explained by flower constancy, Handrkov field experiments only (no literature data). Quasibinomial GLM, F(2, 22) = 9.2, p = 0.001. Honeybee 0.82 (4 plant pairs), bumblebees 0.27 (7 tests, 3 Bombus species), hoverflies 0.28 (14 tests, 6 species, mostly Eristalis). Points = one pollinator species on one plant pair. Bridge to Part 3: a meadow served by inconstant hoverflies should load stigmas with foreign pollen. So what actually lands on a Succisa stigma? Manuscript is an early draft; numbers may change.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Faithful to which flowers?
≈ 1 min







The flower pair matters as much as the pollinator.



Share of decisions due to flower constancy (%) · each cell one pollinator species tested on one plant pair · Handrkov field experiments, Sedláčková (2024)


Same 25 tests as the previous slide, now split by pollinator species and plant pair. Grey = not tested. The same pair, different pollinators: on Centaurea × Succisa constancy ranges from 10 % (Sericomyia) and 15 % (B. pascuorum) to 53 % (honeybee). The same pollinator, different pairs: Eristalis tenax 17 % on Achillea × Angelica but 74 % on Crepis × Succisa; E. interruptus 0–38 %. Quasibinomial GLM with pollinator species and plant pair: entered first, plant pair explains 77 % of the deviance (F = 12.9, p = 0.006) and pollinator species adds 20 % (p = 0.08); in the other order pollinator species explains 61 % and pair still adds 35 % (p = 0.03). Few tests per cell, so treat as indicative. Meaning: constancy is a property of the pollinator × flower combination. Flowers that look alike to a pollinator (Achillea, Angelica: white umbels) are swapped freely; contrasting flowers (Crepis yellow vs Succisa violet) are kept apart.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: How pure are the loads in the field?
text:
How pure are the loads in the field?
≈ 1 min






Honeybees and Halictidae carry almost only their plant (median > 90 %) · large hoverflies (Eristalis interruptus, Helophilus) only 30–40 %


Share of the catch plant’s pollen in each insect’s load · 617 insects, 33 groups (n ≥ 10), Handrkov 2020–2021 · data Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Own-pollen share = proportion of the pollen of the plant the insect was caught on, from the composition counts (slozeni_pylu_proc). Points: individuals; dots and bars: median and interquartile range. Hoverfly groups in bold. Medians: Apis 94 %, Halictidae 95 %, Tachinidae 88 %, Melanostoma 84 %, Syritta 84 %; Eristalis tenax 62 %, E. pertinax 60 %, Bombus 46–65 %; Helophilus trivittatus 42 %, H. pendulus 42 %, Episyrphus 35 %, E. interruptus 32 %; Pieris 0 %, Coenonympha 7 % (butterflies carry few grains). Bridge: the field loads agree with the choice experiments. The large hoverflies that switch flowers in the experiments also carry mixed loads, so the low constancy is not only an artefact of the arena. Not all hoverflies: small Melanostoma, Syritta and Chrysogaster carry fairly pure loads.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: The carrier sets the amount, the flower sets the purity
text:
The carrier sets the amount, the flower sets the purity
≈ 0.5 min






Mixed models with random pollinator group and catch plant · 618 insects, Handrkov 2020–2021 · data Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Variance components: log pollen load ~ (1|group) + (1|catch plant): group 50 %, plant 2 %, residual 47 %. Logit own-pollen share: group 10 %, plant 31 %, residual 59 %. How much pollen an insect carries is a property of the insect (size, hairiness). How pure the load is depends mostly on the plant: some plants (Apiaceae, Ranunculus) are visited by many insects that come from and go to other flowers. This matches the constancy matrix on the previous slides: the flower pair matters as much as the pollinator. Time of day (pooled): neither load (p = 0.73) nor purity (p = 0.68) changes with hour.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Visits are not pollen
≈ 1 min






Visits: Handrkov transects 2020–2021 (6 978 visits) · pollen: 531 swabbed insects · data Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


For the 15 best-sampled pollinator groups, compare the share of their visits to each plant (left) with the share of each plant’s pollen in their loads (right). Groups are ordered by how well the two profiles agree (top = least agreement): - Top: Lucilia and Sarcophagidae visit Sanguisorba frequently, yet carry primarily Selinum and Daucus pollen. Helophilus pendulus visits Succisa but carries Potentilla. - Bottom: Apis and Bombus lapidarius match closely (overlap 0.88 and 0.85). Takeaway: What an insect visits does not dictate what it carries.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
From body to stigma
≈ 1 min




Pollen on the body



>




Pollen on the stigma




Define terms once: conspecific pollen (CP) = own species; heterospecific pollen (HP) = other species. Single-visit deposition (SVD) = what one visit leaves. Terminal pollen deposition (TPD) = the final load on an old stigma. Focal species from now on: Succisa pratensis, a core species of the meadow network (Part 4).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Defining the deposition steps
≈ 1 min



1. Pollinator Body Load





CP (Conspecific)





HP (Heterospecific)




Pollen carried by visitor.Can be own species (CP) or foreign (HP).




2. Single Visit (SVD)





Pollen left by one visit on virgin stigma.Mechanically inefficient & noisy (high CV).




3. Terminal Load (TPD)





Final cumulative load on old stigma.Accumulated visits buffer noise (low CV).




Define terms explicitly: - CP = Conspecific Pollen (own species) - HP = Heterospecific Pollen (foreign pollen from neighbours) - SVD = Single-Visit Deposition: measured experimentally with virgin bagged stigmas exposed to exactly 1 visit. - TPD = Terminal Pollen Deposition: the final load on naturally pollinated stigmas.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
How we measure deposition
≈ 1 min

 Petr ŠvandaMSc graduate, Charles University




Single visit (SVD)



Bag the inflorescence in tulle before anthers open
Unbag when stigmas are receptive
Wait for one visit, note the visitor
Collect the visited stigma into ethanol








Terminal load (TPD)



Flowers with withered corolla = end of stigma life
3 stigmas per head, 30 plants per day
Clear, stain with safranin, squash
Count own and foreign grains at 400×



 




SVD: 124 controlled single visits on virgin stigmas, 2022–2024. If the insect visited more than one flower, only the first stigma was kept. TPD: 693 terminal-stage stigmas from 273 plants, 2022–2024. Slide preparation: 10 % KOH, 3 % H2O2, 8 % acetic acid, then safranin–glycerol, squash under a coverslip, seal with nail polish. Micrograph: Succisa stigma with large own pollen grains and smaller foreign grains. Own and foreign grains are told apart by size, shape and surface ornamentation. The Slavkovský les stigmas were processed the same way.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
One visit is a lottery
≈ 1.5 min




























One visit leaves only ≈ 2 % of the body’s own pollen on the stigma · no difference among Eristalis, Helophilus and Bombus


SVD experiments 2022–2024 on bagged Succisa inflorescences (124 single visits; 300 pollinators swabbed for body loads). Mean body load: CP 148 grains (SD 394), HP 479 (SD 1 102). Only about 2.3 % of body CP and 0.1 % of body HP end up on the stigma in one visit. Kruskal–Wallis among dominant morphogroups: CP H3 = 1.59, p = 0.66; HP H3 = 5.20, p = 0.16. Per visit, the pollinators are functionally equivalent, which fits the Freudenfeld result: what matters is how many visits, not who makes them.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: But the final load is stable
text:
But the final load is stable
≈ 1.5 min











































CV of conspecific pollen: body 129 % → single visit 206 % → terminal load 69 %. Heterospecific pollen stays variable: body 264 % → terminal 147 %. Variance partitioning of TPD (693 stigmas, 273 plants, 2022–2024): years and days explain little CP variance; plants 15 %, stigmas 82 %. Within 2024, days were not significant (CP χ² = 1.32, p = 0.52). HP is different: year (χ² = 32.4, p < 0.001) and plant (χ² = 104.7, p < 0.001) both matter.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
The law of large numbers
≈ 1.5 min













Monte Carlo simulation parameterised by empirical SVD and visitation rates: accumulation of many independent, noisy visits is sufficient to reproduce the stable terminal CP loads observed in the field. HP is different: not predicted by the null model, depends on the floral neighbourhood, and is diluted by high conspecific floral density. Štenc et al., submitted to New Phytologist.

From one meadow to a landscape

Slavkovský les Protected Landscape Area, W Bohemia · land cover ESA WorldCover 2021 · relief AWS Terrain Tiles · boundary © OpenStreetMap

Each meadow sampled once: 37 in 2022, 23 in 2023. Field work: MSc thesis of Natálie Hanusová (2024), supervised by J. Štenc.

Pollen lands on the stigma




A compatible grain germinates: a tube grows down the style to the ovule

What we measured Height of every flowering stalk (194 stalks, 100 plants) Pollen grains and pollen tubes on 61 stigmas from 32 plants

Height, pollen and pollen tubes
≈ 2 min








Most plants are 25–40 cm tall · only 3 % of stalks exceed 50 cm


Pollen per stigma rises with height and levels off at ≈ 50 cm · grey bars = plant heights in the meadow


Pollen tubes follow a flatter curve, peaking at ≈ 45 cm


The share of grains with a tube falls: ≈ 45 % at 15 cm → ≈ 24 % at 65 cm



2026 · with Klára Hodánková and Javier Valverde · unpublished


Step 1: context. Height of 194 flowering stalks on 100 plants, median 32 cm; about 60 % are 25–40 cm, only 3 % above 50 cm. So most plants sit on the rising part of the next curve. Step 2: own pollen per stigma ~ quadratic height, negative binomial GLMM with plant/flower random effects: linear z = 4.2, p < 0.001; quadratic z = −3.6, p < 0.001; predicted peak at about 50 cm. The tall end rests on few plants. Step 3: number of pollen tubes ~ quadratic height (Poisson GLMM): linear p = 0.32, quadratic p = 0.014, peak at about 45 cm. No confidence band shown for this curve; the model’s interval is not informative. Step 4: proportion of grains with a tube ~ height (binomial GLMM): β = −0.019 per cm, p = 0.041. Take-home: taller plants get more pollen, but a smaller share of it germinates. Possible reasons: more self or related pollen from long visits on tall plants, competition among grains, or older stigmas. One season, one site: a lead to follow, not a result.

Pollen deposition through a flower’s life
≈ 2 min













Literature synthesis: 36 species, 23 families, 49 surveys, 194 time-stamped records · Štenc (in prep.)


Meta-analysis of published deposition time series (Štenc, in prep.). Left: what the AUC is. Deposition scaled to the survey maximum, flower age scaled to maximum longevity; AUC = area under that curve (trapezoidal rule). Right: AUC per survey. Self-incompatible species accumulate pollen over a broader part of flower life (median AUC 0.72 vs 0.14 in SIC; Wilcoxon, BH-adjusted p = 0.024) but rarely reach P/O ≥ 1 (1 of 7 surveys). Divided by the covered span, the mean level does not differ (0.77 vs 0.71, p = 0.82). Part of the AUC gap is sampling coverage. Step 2 (click): highest pollen:ovule ratio reached on the stigma in each survey. Below the dashed line there are fewer grains than ovules, so not all ovules can be fertilised. SIC: 14 of 16 exceed it, often 10–100×, within a short sampling window. Self-incompatible species keep accumulating but stay pollen-limited. What is the core?
≈ 1 min



Photo: Colin, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0






All plants






Peel weakly linked plants






What remains = core





k-core decomposition (Seidman 1983), done separately for each year. Think of an onion: remove plants with few sharing links, repeat until only a mutually connected centre remains. A species counts as core if it is central more often than expected from its flower abundance (null model, 1 000 permutations per year).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
A stable core
≈ 1.5 min






k-core decomposition per year, null model of 1 000 permutations per year. Six species are central in the sharing network across 15 years: Centaurea jacea, Selinum carvifolia, Succisa pratensis, Pimpinella saxifraga, Achillea ptarmica, Ranunculus acris. Plant identity explains 38 % of centrality variance beyond floral abundance (44 %). Note that the two best-studied species of Parts 2 and 3, Succisa and Centaurea, are both core species.

text:
Who drives whom?
≈ 1 min







The core feeds the pollinators that everyone else shares.



Müller’s index of potential for apparent competition (PAC), per year 2011–2025 · species present ≥ 10 years · point = mean, bar = interquartile range


PAC is directional. PAC(A → B) is high when the pollinators visiting B get most of their food from A, so A’s flowers “drive” B’s visitors. Net role = outgoing − incoming PAC. All six core species are net drivers (Centaurea +3.9, Succisa +2.4, A. ptarmica +2.4, R. acris +2.1, Pimpinella +2.0, Selinum +1.6). Core species are drivers in 91 % of species-years, peripheral species in 12 %. Only Sanguisorba comes close among the rest. Meaning: the peripheral plants are visited by pollinators that the core keeps alive. For pollen this means foreign pollen on peripheral stigmas will mostly be core pollen, and the core receives little foreign pollen in return.

text:
The price of being in the core
≈ 1.5 min









Hypothesis: when drought crowds pollinators onto the core, core plants share almost every insect and receive more foreign pollen.


First hint on Succisa stigmas: own pollen stable, foreign pollen highest in dry 2023, lowest in 2024 when Succisa flowered densely.

section: Who wins from splitting the day?
text:
Who wins from splitting the day?
≈ 1 min


Reduction in apparent competition from diurnal stratification · 15-year mean (2011–2025) · DiuHanPolNet


Who gains the most from splitting the day? 1. In plants, the biggest winners are the peripheral species: Lathyrus pratensis (−45%), Trifolium pratense (−37%), Lotus corniculatus (−36%), and Potentilla erecta (−33%). These are the exact species that were dominated in space! By foraging at temporal fringes (morning and afternoon), they escape the midday bully rush and cut their apparent competition by more than a third. 2. The core drivers (Centaurea jacea, Succisa pratensis) gain the least (−8%). They don’t need to hide: they dominate the crowded midday hours. 3. In pollinators, subordinate foragers (Zygaena moths −45%, muscid flies −32%, small hoverflies −28%) escape dominant competitors (Apis, Bombus −12% to −13%) by using temporal refuges. Space and time act as orthogonal escape routes for biodiversity.

text:
Timing decides what pollinators carry
≈ 1.5 min







Own pollen on Succisa visitors: ≈ 350 grains at 8:30 → ≈ 50 at 14:30


Foreign pollen stays the same all day


A morning visitor carries ≈ 50 % own pollen, an afternoon visitor ≈ 7 %



293 swabbed visitors of Succisa, Handrkov 2024 · confirms Štenc et al. (2025) with new data


This brings the community result back to pollen. Swabs (same method as before) from insects caught on Succisa through the day in 2024. Own pollen ~ hour: quasi-Poisson slope −0.33 per hour, p < 0.001. Foreign pollen ~ hour: slope 0.01, p = 0.88. Share of own pollen ~ hour: quasi-binomial slope −0.44 per hour, p < 0.001. Single visits to virgin stigmas (124 visits, 2022–2024) also left the most own pollen at 8:00 (≈ 9 grains vs ≈ 2 later), but the trend is only marginal (p = 0.07). Meaning: Succisa’s morning release is not a curiosity. Visits in the first hours move most of its own pollen; later visits mostly bring foreign pollen. title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Where a plant grows matters
≈ 1 min



Clumps attract visitors; dense neighbours take them away.



Fine-scale 1 m² mapping of flowers in 93 plots × 16 years, 86 plant species · HanSpaNet (in prep.)


After time, space. In every plot we map flowers at 1 m² resolution, so for each plant species we know how many flowers it has, how clumped they are, and how many and how mixed its neighbours are. Mixed model: log visitation rate per species × plot × year ~ own abundance + own clumping + neighbour density + neighbour clumping + neighbour heterogeneity + ESI, random year, plot and species; n = 14 718; all predictors standardised (per 1 SD). Own abundance +0.54, own clumping +0.16 (both p < 0.001); neighbour density −0.06 (p < 0.001). Neighbour clumping (−0.01, p = 0.18) and heterogeneity (−0.01, p = 0.51) are not significant with the current data (the draft manuscript reported p = 0.012 and 0.048; to be checked). So: be many and be together; a crowd of other flowers around you “steals” visits. Some species (Succisa, Centaurea) are thieves: attractive and resilient to neighbours.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Space shapes apparent competition
≈ 1 min



Identity sets the driver; dense clumps and flower numbers deliver the blow.



Dyadic mixed model across 96,364 co-occurring plant pairs in 93 plots × 15 years · PAC × HanSpaNet


Does space affect the potential for apparent competition (PAC), and how? We tested pairwise apparent competition (PAC from neighbour to focal plant) across 96,364 co-occurring pairs in 93 plots over 15 years, controlling for donor species, recipient species, and year random effects. 1. Neighbour identity is by far the biggest effect (+0.40 SD, p < 10⁻⁸): when a neighbour is one of the dominant “thieves” (Succisa or Centaurea), apparent competition on the focal plant surges. 2. Neighbour abundance (+0.08 SD, p < 10⁻¹²⁰): having more flowers than the focal plant consistently increases the pressure. 3. Spatial clumping (+0.033 SD, p < 10⁻²⁷): independent of flower abundance, a neighbour growing in dense clumps exerts significantly stronger apparent competition than an evenly dispersed neighbour. 4. Focal plant clumping (+0.028 SD, p < 10⁻¹⁹): dense focal clumps also draw in shared generalist foragers. So apparent competition is not just a whole-meadow property: it is physically structured by fine-scale floral clumps.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Who wins and who loses in space?
text:
Who wins and who loses in space?
≈ 1 min



Core drivers dictate the visitors; the periphery pays the price.



Species-level driver power minus vulnerability from dyadic mixed models · 96,364 pairs across 93 plots × 15 years


When we map species along their net competitive role in space (driver power minus target vulnerability): 1. The clear WINNERS: Centaurea jacea, Succisa pratensis, Achillea ptarmica, Ranunculus acris, Selinum carvifolia. These are the core species. They have massive baseline attractiveness, form dense clumps, and their target vulnerability is negative—meaning they are immune to neighbour competition. When they clump, they monopolize dominant pollinators and dictate who else gets visited. 2. The LOSERS: Hypericum perforatum, Stellaria graminea, Galium uliginosum, Lotus corniculatus, Cuscuta europaea, Prunella vulgaris. These peripheral species have positive vulnerability: whenever a neighbour clumps nearby, their visits are stolen and they receive heavy heterospecific pollen loads, while exerting almost no competitive pressure back.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Untangling the drivers: what are we testing?
text:
Untangling the drivers: what are we testing?
≈ 1 min



Question


We know that time (hour, date), space (clumping, neighbours), and years all matter. In nature, however, all operate simultaneously. What is a direct driver, and what is merely an indirect consequence?




Sampling Unit


45,795 interactions across 15 years (2011–2025) sliced into: 3,588 localized sessions (1 of 93 permanent plots × day in August × 3-h diurnal block) In each session, we observe exactly who visits whom.




Symmetrical Test


RDA Variance Partitioning across 5 candidate driver sets:


Year (interannual climate & cycles)


Date (August phenology)


Hour (diurnal timing)


Meadow position (X, Y topography)


The other partner (floral / visitor mix)



Symmetrically testing: Who visits? vs What is visited?






Do insects choose the space, or do they only follow the flowers?



Transition from fine-scale space to community-wide synthesis. We saw the effect of time of day (Part 1). We saw that years differ wildly in who is abundant (Part 2). And we just saw that within-meadow spatial neighbourhood strongly modulates visits (Part 2 space slide). The big question: when all these drivers act together, who drives what? For example: does meadow space directly dictate which hoverflies or bees visit a plot (spatial microhabitat, wind, shelter), or does space only matter because different plants grow in different parts of the meadow? Dataset: 15 continuous years (2011–2025) of diurnal surveys at Handrkov, 93 permanent plots mapped with precise coordinates. We slice the data into 3,588 observation units: one plot on one day in one part of the day (morning, midday, afternoon, evening), filtering for at least 5 visits. Method: Redundancy Analysis (RDA) variance partitioning on Hellinger-transformed community matrices. We test 5 sets of predictors: Year (factor), Season (date polynomial), Hour of day (polynomial), Meadow position (cubic trend surface of X and Y), and the composition of the interacting partner (PCA axes). We run this symmetrically in two directions: 1. Explaining the pollinator community (“Who visits?”) 2. Explaining which flowers receive visits (“What is visited?”) By partitioning the variation, we isolate the unique fraction (what that driver explains alone) from the shared fraction (indirect pathways).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: Year, season, hour, space: what drives what?
text:
Year, season, hour, space: what drives what?
≈ 1.5 min





dark = explained by that driver alone · light = shared with other drivers


45 795 visits · 3 588 samples (plot × day × part of day) · 93 plots · August 2011–2025, Handrkov · RDA variance partitioning


Each sample is one plot on one day in one part of the day (7–10, 11–13, 14–16, 17–19 h), with at least 5 visits. Response: Hellinger-transformed composition of pollinators (106 taxa) or of visited plants (29 taxa). Drivers: year (factor), date within the August survey (quadratic), hour (quadratic), position of the plot (cubic trend of x/y coordinates) and the composition of the other partner (PCA axes). Adjusted R² from RDA; unique fraction = loss of adjusted R² when that driver is dropped. Who visits (30 % in total): year 13 % (6.5 % alone), plants visited 21 % (8 % alone), position 9 % but only 0.6 % alone, i.e. space works through the plants. Date 2 %, hour 1 %. What is visited (49 % in total): position 30 % (11 % alone), pollinators 32 % (10 % alone), year 12 % (3.5 % alone). Date 2 %, hour 1 %. Hour is small at the community level because the same taxa are active all day; its effect is in who visits which plant at which hour (the earlier slides), not in which taxa are present.

text:
The system in one picture
≈ 1 min



Years set the pollinators, space sets the flowers, and the two meet in the network.



Arrows show the unique fractions from the previous slide (variance partitioning, not causal paths). Pollinator composition follows the year (6.5 %) and which flowers are open (8 %); space reaches pollinators only through the plants (0.6 % alone). title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Outlook: Beyond static networks
≈ 1 min







Every link in the network is governed by a different axis of nature.



Dyadic variance partitioning of apparent competition (608 plant–plant links) · Handrkov 2011–2025 · Štenc et al. (in prep.)


Novel conceptual framework: Instead of asking what the network looks like as a static graph, we deconstruct what DRIVES each link. 1. Network modularity is not just a topological artifact—modules are governed by different physical dimensions! 2. Spatial aggregation governs the core (76% space): Dominant composites (Centaurea, Succisa) are bound by micro-spatial clumping within plots. 3. Climate volatility governs the generalist bridges (up to 44% year): White umbels (Heracleum, Daucus) link modules via boom-and-bust insect years. 4. Diurnal phenology buffers the subordinates (-45% PAC): Subordinate legumes (Lathyrus, Trifolium) escape spatial bullies via morning temporal refuges. Every edge in an ecological network has its own mechanistic driver profile.

Not in a vacuum

Pollination does not happen as an isolated interaction between one flower and one dedicated visitor. In species-rich meadows, dozens of plants co-flower and share the same pollinator guild. Every visit is embedded in a complex web of direct and indirect interactions.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Pollen presentation theory
≈ 1 min






Pollen Presentation Theory: Harder and Thomson (1989) · diminishing returns of pollen removal


Harder & Thomson 1989 (American Naturalist): Evolutionary options for maximizing pollen dispersal of animal-pollinated plants. Single-visit pollen removal has diminishing returns: when an insect removes large amounts of pollen at once (“dumping”), a huge fraction is groomed away into scopae/corbiculae, eaten, or buried on the body. Restricting the amount removed per visit (“dosing”) operates on the steep, highly efficient part of the curve, maximizing the proportion of pollen reaching conspecific stigmas.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
section: But does it reflect pollen transfer?
text:
But does it reflect pollen transfer?
≈ 0.5 min

But does visitation reflect actual pollen transfer?


We have seen that visitation matches diurnal pollen availability (START I, Štenc et al. 2023). But does a visit equal pollination? Observing visits only tells us who lands on flowers. It doesn’t tell us: 1. Whether pollen is actually picked up. 2. How many grains the insect carries (load). 3. How pure that pollen load is (conspecific vs heterospecific). To bridge the gap between flower visitation and actual pollen flow, we captured foraging insects and swabbed their bodies. This brings us to START II (Štenc et al. 2025, PPEES).

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Community transport vs visits
≈ 1 min









Visits ≠ Pollen flow — flower visits drastically overestimate transport for Succisa & Sanguisorba, but double-underestimate Selinum & Potentilla.



Pollen loads reweighted to each group’s visit distribution · Handrkov 2020–2021 · Freudenfeld et al. (2025)


Here we compare each plant species’ share of community flower visits (grey) against its share of all carried pollen (rose).

The discrepancies:


Centaurea and Ranunculus are balanced (they get ~26% and ~18% of visits and move ~29% and ~18% of pollen).
Selinum and Potentilla are massively over-represented: they get only 7% and 5% of visits, but account for 14% and 9% of all transported pollen (+2×).
Conversely, Succisa, Sanguisorba, and Trifolium are severely under-represented: Succisa gets 11% of visits but only 4% of transported pollen (3× less); Sanguisorba gets 8% visits but 3% pollen; Trifolium gets 3% visits but under 0.5% pollen (7× less).


What does this mean?


Traditional plant-pollinator networks based solely on visits assume that every visit moves pollen equally. This assumption fails: visit networks overestimate transport for plants like Succisa, while drastically underestimating transport for plants like Selinum.
Visit frequency does not equal functional pollen transport.


The effect of pollen production (Future testing):


A crucial open question is pollen production: Does an umbel of Selinum dominate the pollen pool simply because it produces orders of magnitude more pollen grains than a Succisa head?
In future work, we are directly measuring pollen production per flower/inflorescence across all species to disentangle the effect of sheer grain abundance from flower morphology and insect grooming.

Literature synthesis: 36 species, 23 families, 49 surveys, 194 time-stamped records · Štenc (in prep.)


Meta-analysis of published deposition time series (Štenc, in prep.). Left: what the AUC is. Deposition scaled to the survey maximum, flower age scaled to maximum longevity; AUC = area under that curve (trapezoidal rule). Right: AUC per survey. Self-incompatible species accumulate pollen over a broader part of flower life (median AUC 0.72 vs 0.14 in SIC; Wilcoxon, BH-adjusted p = 0.024) but rarely reach P/O ≥ 1 (1 of 7 surveys). CAVEAT: SIC surveys typically have 2 time points covering ~20 % of flower life, SI surveys 5 points covering the whole life. Divided by the covered span, the mean level does not differ (0.77 vs 0.71, p = 0.82). Part of the AUC gap is sampling coverage. ≈ 1 min







The core feeds the pollinators that everyone else shares.



Müller’s index of potential for apparent competition (PAC), per year 2011–2025 · species present ≥ 10 years · point = mean, bar = interquartile range


PAC is directional. PAC(A → B) is high when the pollinators visiting B get most of their food from A, so A’s flowers “drive” B’s visitors. Net role = outgoing − incoming PAC. All six core species are net drivers (Centaurea +3.9, Succisa +2.4, A. ptarmica +2.4, R. acris +2.1, Pimpinella +2.0, Selinum +1.6). Core species are drivers in 91 % of species-years, peripheral species in 12 %. Only Sanguisorba comes close among the rest. Meaning: the peripheral plants are visited by pollinators that the core keeps alive. For pollen this means foreign pollen on peripheral stigmas will mostly be core pollen, and the core receives little foreign pollen in return.

After time, space. In every plot we map flowers at 1 m² resolution, so for each plant species we know how many flowers it has, how clumped they are, and how many and how mixed its neighbours are. Mixed model: log visitation rate per species × plot × year ~ own abundance + own clumping + neighbour density + neighbour clumping + neighbour heterogeneity + ESI, random year, plot and species; n = 14 718; all predictors standardised (per 1 SD). Own abundance +0.54, own clumping +0.16 (both p < 0.001); neighbour density −0.06 (p < 0.001). So: be many and be together; a crowd of other flowers around you “steals” visits. Some species (Succisa, Centaurea) are thieves: attractive and resilient to neighbours.

Identity sets the driver; dense clumps and flower numbers deliver the blow.



Dyadic mixed model across 96,364 co-occurring plant pairs in 93 plots × 15 years · PAC × HanSpaNet


Does space affect the potential for apparent competition (PAC), and how? We tested pairwise apparent competition (PAC from neighbour to focal plant) across 96,364 co-occurring pairs in 93 plots over 15 years, controlling for donor species, recipient species, and year random effects. 1. Neighbour identity is by far the biggest effect (+0.40 SD, p < 10⁻⁸): when a neighbour is one of the dominant “thieves” (Succisa or Centaurea), apparent competition on the focal plant surges. 2. Neighbour abundance (+0.08 SD, p < 10⁻¹²⁰): having more flowers than the focal plant consistently increases the pressure. 3. Spatial clumping (+0.033 SD, p < 10⁻²⁷): independent of flower abundance, a neighbour growing in dense clumps exerts significantly stronger apparent competition than an evenly dispersed neighbour. 4. Focal plant clumping (+0.028 SD, p < 10⁻¹⁹): dense focal clumps also draw in shared generalist foragers. So apparent competition is not just a whole-meadow property: it is physically structured by fine-scale floral clumps.

Backup: Who wins and who loses in space?
≈ 1 min



Core drivers dictate the visitors; the periphery pays the price.



Species-level driver power minus vulnerability from dyadic mixed models · 96,364 pairs across 93 plots × 15 years


When we map species along their net competitive role in space (driver power minus target vulnerability): 1. The clear WINNERS: Centaurea jacea, Succisa pratensis, Achillea ptarmica, Ranunculus acris, Selinum carvifolia. These are the core species. They have massive baseline attractiveness, form dense clumps, and their target vulnerability is negative—meaning they are immune to neighbour competition. When they clump, they monopolize dominant pollinators and dictate who else gets visited. 2. The LOSERS: Hypericum perforatum, Stellaria graminea, Galium uliginosum, Lotus corniculatus, Cuscuta europaea, Prunella vulgaris. These peripheral species have positive vulnerability: whenever a neighbour clumps nearby, their visits are stolen and they receive heavy heterospecific pollen loads, while exerting almost no competitive pressure back.

Backup: Untangling the drivers: what are we testing?
≈ 1 min



Question


We know that time (hour, date), space (clumping, neighbours), and years all matter. In nature, however, all operate simultaneously. What is a direct driver, and what is merely an indirect consequence?




Sampling Unit


45,795 interactions across 15 years (2011–2025) sliced into: 3,588 localized sessions (1 of 93 permanent plots × day in August × 3-h diurnal block) In each session, we observe exactly who visits whom.




Symmetrical Test


RDA Variance Partitioning across 5 candidate driver sets:


Year (interannual climate & cycles)


Date (August phenology)


Hour (diurnal timing)


Meadow position (X, Y topography)


The other partner (floral / visitor mix)



Symmetrically testing: Who visits? vs What is visited?






Do insects choose the space, or do they only follow the flowers?



Transition from fine-scale space to community-wide synthesis. We saw the effect of time of day (Part 1). We saw that years differ wildly in who is abundant (Part 2). And we just saw that within-meadow spatial neighbourhood strongly modulates visits (Part 2 space slide). The big question: when all these drivers act together, who drives what? For example: does meadow space directly dictate which hoverflies or bees visit a plot (spatial microhabitat, wind, shelter), or does space only matter because different plants grow in different parts of the meadow? Dataset: 15 continuous years (2011–2025) of diurnal surveys at Handrkov, 93 permanent plots mapped with precise coordinates. We slice the data into 3,588 observation units: one plot on one day in one part of the day (morning, midday, afternoon, evening), filtering for at least 5 visits. Method: Redundancy Analysis (RDA) variance partitioning on Hellinger-transformed community matrices. We test 5 sets of predictors: Year (factor), Season (date polynomial), Hour of day (polynomial), Meadow position (cubic trend surface of X and Y), and the composition of the interacting partner (PCA axes). We run this symmetrically in two directions: 1. Explaining the pollinator community (“Who visits?”) 2. Explaining which flowers receive visits (“What is visited?”) By partitioning the variation, we isolate the unique fraction (what that driver explains alone) from the shared fraction (indirect pathways).

dark = explained by that driver alone · light = shared with other drivers


45 795 visits · 3 588 samples (plot × day × part of day) · 93 plots · August 2011–2025, Handrkov · RDA variance partitioning


Each sample is one plot on one day in one part of the day (7–10, 11–13, 14–16, 17–19 h), with at least 5 visits. Response: Hellinger-transformed composition of pollinators (106 taxa) or of visited plants (29 taxa). Drivers: year (factor), date within the August survey (quadratic), hour (quadratic), position of the plot (cubic trend of x/y coordinates) and the composition of the other partner (PCA axes). Adjusted R² from RDA; unique fraction = loss of adjusted R² when that driver is dropped. Who visits (30 % in total): year 13 % (6.5 % alone), plants visited 21 % (8 % alone), position 9 % but only 0.6 % alone, i.e. space works through the plants. Date 2 %, hour 1 %. What is visited (49 % in total): position 30 % (11 % alone), pollinators 32 % (10 % alone), year 12 % (3.5 % alone). Date 2 %, hour 1 %. Hour is small at the community level because the same taxa are active all day; its effect is in who visits which plant at which hour (the earlier slides), not in which taxa are present.

Years set the pollinators, space sets the flowers, and the two meet in the network.



Arrows show the unique fractions from the previous slide (variance partitioning, not causal paths). Pollinator composition follows the year (6.5 %) and which flowers are open (8 %); space reaches pollinators only through the plants (0.6 % alone). Which plants get visited follows where they grow (11 %) and who is around (10 %); year matters less (3.5 %). Date within August and hour of day explain < 1 % of composition alone: they reshape the timing of interactions (the time-of-day slides), not the identity of partners.

Backup: Outlook: Beyond static networks
≈ 1 min







Every link in the network is governed by a different axis of nature.



Dyadic variance partitioning of apparent competition (608 plant–plant links) · Handrkov 2011–2025 · Štenc et al. (in prep.)


Novel conceptual framework: Instead of asking what the network looks like as a static graph, we deconstruct what DRIVES each link. 1. Network modularity is not just a topological artifact—modules are governed by different physical dimensions! 2. Spatial aggregation governs the core (76% space): Dominant composites (Centaurea, Succisa) are bound by micro-spatial clumping within plots. 3. Climate volatility governs the generalist bridges (up to 44% year): White umbels (Heracleum, Daucus) link modules via boom-and-bust insect years. 4. Diurnal phenology buffers the subordinates (-45% PAC): Subordinate legumes (Lathyrus, Trifolium) escape spatial bullies via morning temporal refuges. Every edge in an ecological network has its own mechanistic driver profile.

Own pollen on Succisa visitors: ≈ 350 grains at 8:30 → ≈ 50 at 14:30


Foreign pollen stays the same all day


A morning visitor carries ≈ 50 % own pollen, an afternoon visitor ≈ 7 %



293 swabbed visitors of Succisa, Handrkov 2024 · confirms Štenc et al. (2025) with new data


This brings the community result back to pollen. Swabs (same method as before) from insects caught on Succisa through the day in 2024. Own pollen ~ hour: quasi-Poisson slope −0.33 per hour, p < 0.001. Foreign pollen ~ hour: slope 0.01, p = 0.88. Share of own pollen ~ hour: quasi-binomial slope −0.44 per hour, p < 0.001. Single visits to virgin stigmas (124 visits, 2022–2024) also left the most own pollen at 8:00 (≈ 9 grains vs ≈ 2 later), but the trend is only marginal (p = 0.07). Meaning: Succisa’s morning release is not a curiosity. Visits in the first hours move most of its own pollen; later visits mostly bring foreign pollen. Next step: hour-by-hour pollen-transfer networks, combining the diurnal network with swabs and stigma loads, to see which pollen moves between which plants and when.

title: Seminar Göteborg 2026
text:
Three axes of ecological interactions
≈ 1 min



 


SPACE


where you grow




   


YEAR


the climate you face




 


TIME


when you flower





What actually governs each interaction: space, year, or time?



Up until now, networks have mostly been viewed as static webs. In reality, interactions vary across three fundamental physical dimensions: 1. Space: micro-spatial clumping within plots. 2. Year: macro-climate shocks and boom-and-bust population dynamics across 15 seasons. 3. Time: diurnal phenology and hourly schedules. The question is: does the entire network respond as a whole, or is each pairwise interaction governed by a different axis?
